entry: [[Polynomial]] equation of degree three. A cubic equation in one variable has the form ax³ + bx² + cx + d = 0, in which a is not zero. If the coefficients are real, it has at least one real root. Cubic equations were known to the ancient Babylonians, Greeks, Chinese, Indians, and Egyptians. [[Gerolamo Cardano]] published the complete formula in his 1545 treatise *Ars Magna*, expressing the roots through square roots and cube roots.

Early 20th-century [[Avant-garde|avant-garde]] art movement that began in [[Paris]]. Cubist subjects are analyzed, broken up, and reassembled in abstract form, depicted from multiple perspectives rather than a single viewpoint. The movement was pioneered by [[Pablo Picasso]] and Georges Braque, and one primary influence was the representation of three-dimensional form in the late works of [[Paul Cézanne]]. Cubism revolutionized painting and the visual arts and sparked innovations in music, ballet, literature, and architecture. It introduced [[Collage|collage]] as a modern art form. Analytic Cubism, from 1910 to 1912, was followed by Synthetic Cubism, which favored simpler shapes and brighter colors. Cubism has been considered the most influential art movement of the 20th century, and [[Futurism]], [[Dada]], and [[Art Deco]] developed in response to it.

Ancient unit of length based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger. It was used primarily by the [[Sumer|Sumerians]] and [[Ancient Egypt|Egyptians]], and the [[Bible]] mentions cubits in accounts of Noah's Ark and the [[Ark of the Covenant]]. The common cubit was divided into six palms or 24 digits, and the royal cubit into seven palms or 28 digits. Lengths typically ranged from 44.4 to 52.92 cm. The ancient Egyptian royal cubit is the earliest attested standard measure, and surviving cubit rods range from 523.5 to 529.2 mm in length. The term is still used in hedgelaying, where the length of the forearm sets the spacing of stakes.

Husband of an adulterous wife. The wife of an adulterous husband is called a cuckquean. In [[Biology|biology]], a cuckold is a male who unwittingly invests parental effort in juveniles that are not genetically his offspring. The word derives from the [[Cuckoo|cuckoo]] bird, alluding to its brood parasitism, or tendency to lay eggs in the nests of other birds. English usage first appears about 1250 in *The Owl and the Nightingale*. [[William Shakespeare]] often referred to cuckolds in his writing.

Family of [[Bird|birds]], the sole taxon in the order Cuculiformes. The family contains 150 species in 33 genera, including the common cuckoo, [[Roadrunner|roadrunners]], koels, malkohas, couas, coucals, and anis. Cuckoos are generally medium-sized and slender. Most species live in trees, though a sizeable minority are ground-dwelling, and the majority are tropical. Some species are migratory, and most species raise their own young. Most Eurasian species are brood parasites that lay their eggs in the nests of other species, giving rise to the metaphorical terms cuckoo's egg and [[Cuckold|cuckold]]. In [[Greek mythology]] cuckoos were sacred to [[Hera]], in [[India]] they are sacred to Kamadeva, the god of desire, and in [[Japan]] the cuckoo symbolizes unrequited love.

Widely cultivated creeping vine whose fruits are eaten as vegetables. The cucumber (*Cucumis sativus*) is an annual plant in the family [[Cucurbitaceae]], with three main types: slicing, pickling, and seedless. It originates in a region of [[Asia]] extending from India, Nepal, Bangladesh, [[China]], and northern Thailand. Cucumbers have been cultivated for at least 3,000 years; the Roman emperor [[Tiberius]] ate them all year round, and [[Charlemagne]] had them grown in the Middle Ages. The Spanish brought them to the Americas in the [[Columbian exchange]] in 1494. Most cultivars need [[Pollination|pollination]] by bees, and the fruit is botanically a berry. In 2024, world production of cucumbers and gherkins was 88 million tonnes, led by China with 78% of the total. [[Carl Linnaeus]] described the species in 1753.

Plant species, also called melon or true melon, with many cultivated varieties. The fruit is a pepo, with flesh that is either sweet or bland, and its rind may be smooth (as in honeydew), ribbed (European cantaloupe), wrinkled (Casaba melon), or netted (American cantaloupe). Melons were domesticated independently four times. Some botanists consider them native to the [[Levant]] and Egypt, while others place their origin in [[Iran]], India, or Central Asia. Melons do not cross with [[Watermelon|watermelon]], [[Cucumber|cucumber]], or [[Pumpkin|pumpkin]]. A raw cantaloupe provides 34 [[Calorie|calories]] per 100 g and is a rich source of vitamins A and C.

Genus of herbaceous plants in the [[Cucurbitaceae|gourd family]], native to the [[Andes]] and [[Mesoamerica]]. Five domesticated species are grown for their flesh and seeds and are variously known as squash, [[Pumpkin|pumpkin]], or gourd. The number of accepted species varies from 13 to 30. Most species are herbaceous vines growing 5 to 15 m in length, with tendrils that help them climb. Each plant bears separate male and female flowers: the female flowers produce fruit and the male flowers produce pollen, which [[Honey bee|honey bees]] visit along with specialist bees. The fruits are good sources of vitamins A and C, and they are used in pumpkin pie, bread, soups, and desserts. Though botanically fruits, squashes are typically cooked and eaten as [[Vegetable|vegetables]].

Plant family of about 965 species in 101 genera, also called cucurbits or the gourd family. Most species are annual vines with tendrils, though some are woody lianas, thorny shrubs, or trees. Many species have large yellow or white flowers, and the fruit is often a modified [[Berry (botany)|berry]] called a pepo. The family ranks among the highest of plant families for the number and percentage of species used as human food. Cultivated members include [[Cucurbita|squashes and pumpkins]], [[Watermelon|watermelon]], [[Cucumber|cucumber]], and luffa, whose fully ripened fibrous fruits become the loofah sponge. One of the oldest fossil cucurbits is *Cucurbitaciphyllum lobatum*, a leaf from the Paleocene epoch found in Montana.

Games of skill played with a cue stick on a cloth-covered table bounded by elastic cushions. Cue sports fall into three major subdivisions. Carom billiards is played on tables without pockets; [[Pool (cue sports)|pool]] is played on six-pocket tables and includes eight-ball, the world's most widely played cue sport, and nine-ball, the dominant professional game; and [[Snooker]], English billiards, and Russian pyramid are played on a larger six-pocket table. Cue sports evolved from outdoor lawn games related to croquet and [[Golf]]. King [[Louis XI]] of France had the first known indoor billiard table, and [[Louis XIV]] further popularized the game among the French nobility.

Style of cooking characterized by distinctive ingredients, techniques, and dishes, usually associated with a specific culture or region. Every cuisine evolves from the resources of its region, and [[Climate|climate]], agriculture, trade routes, and cultural exchanges shape its flavors and practices. Religious food laws also influence cuisine, as in the mainly lacto-vegetarian [[Indian cuisine]] shaped by [[Hinduism]]. Regional ingredients commonly define a cuisine, as Japanese rice does in [[Japanese cuisine]]. Historical exchanges, including the [[Columbian exchange]] and the [[Silk Road]], introduced tomatoes, chilies, and [[Potato|potatoes]] from the Americas, which became essential to several cuisines. Since the late 20th century, [[Globalization|globalization]] has spread restaurants, media, and travel, preserving traditional foodways while fostering fusion cuisine. A cuisine reflects the history, geography, and identity of its people.

Art of preparing, cooking, and presenting food, usually in the form of meals. Expert chefs make meals that are both aesthetically beautiful and delicious, which requires understanding of food science, [[Nutrition|nutrition]], and diet. After [[Restaurant|restaurants]], the principal workplaces include delicatessens, [[Hotel|hotels]], and hospitals. The first cooking school in the United States, the Boston Cooking School, was founded in 1879; it standardized cooking practices and recipes. Le Cordon Bleu in Paris, founded in 1895, followed as a European center of formal training. In the Western world, the craft moved from castle kitchens to inns and hotels after the [[Renaissance]] and then became a field of study.

Social group with unusual and often extreme religious, spiritual, or philosophical beliefs and rituals. Extreme devotion to a particular person, object, or goal is another characteristic often ascribed to cults. The word derives from the Latin *cultus*, meaning worship. In modern English the term is generally pejorative and has been applied to gangs, [[Crime|organized crime]], and terrorist organizations. Sociologists have studied [[New religious movement|new religious movements]] since the 1930s, and since the 1970s the secular anti-cult movement has accused some groups of brainwashing. Scholars disagree on the term's usefulness: some argue it lacks scholarly rigor and is dehumanizing, while others see it as empowering for ex-members of traumatic groups. After the [[Waco siege]], some scholars argued that labeling the Branch Davidians a cult was a significant factor in the deaths. Groups labeled cults range from small local groups to international organizations with up to millions of members.

Idealized and heroic image of a leader, built through flattery and propaganda. Such an image is created through mass media, propaganda, staged spectacles, the arts, [[Patriotism|patriotism]], and government-organized rallies. It resembles apotheosis but uses modern social engineering, and it is usually established by the state or party in one-party states. Cults of personality often accompany totalitarian or authoritarian governments, though they also appear in some monarchies and liberal democracies. The most notorious examples arose in the 20th century, when mass media allowed leaders to project images to the masses, including those of [[Joseph Stalin]] and [[Mao Zedong]]. The [[Internet]] and social media have renewed the phenomenon in the 21st century. Critics argue that regimes construct such cults to avoid accountability, while proponents describe them as organic [[Charisma|charisma]].

Cultivated plant selected for desired traits that it retains when propagated. Cultivars are propagated by division, cuttings, grafting, tissue culture, or controlled seed production. Popular ornamentals such as [[Rose|roses]], [[Camellia|camellias]], [[Rhododendron|rhododendrons]], and [[Azalea|azaleas]] are commonly cultivars, as are almost all of the world's agricultural [[Crop|crops]], which have been selected for yield, flavor, and disease resistance. Since genetic engineering emerged in the 1970s, some food crops have been [[Genetic engineering|genetically engineered]]. Horticulturists generally believe the word was coined to mean cultivated variety. Cultivar names follow the rules of the International Code of Nomenclature for Cultivated Plants, which requires a [[Latin]] botanical name followed by a vernacular epithet.

Farm implement used for [[Tillage|secondary tillage]]. Cultivators stir and pulverize soil before planting to prepare a loose seedbed, or after the [[Crop|crop]] has begun growing to kill weeds. Unlike a [[Harrow (tool)|harrow]], which disturbs the entire soil surface, a cultivator disturbs the soil in careful patterns that spare crop plants. Toothed cultivators resemble chisel plows but work near the surface. Motorized models attach to two-wheel or four-wheel [[Tractor|tractors]], and draft animals still pull them in many developing nations. The powered rotary hoe was invented in [[Australia]] by Arthur Clifford Howard, who began experimenting with rotary tillage in 1912 on his father's farm in New South Wales.

Sociopolitical movement in the [[China|People's Republic of China]], 1966–1976. [[Mao Zedong]] launched it in May 1966, saying that bourgeois elements had infiltrated government and society with the aim of restoring [[Capitalism|capitalism]]. Its stated goal was to advance communism by purging remnants of capitalist and traditional elements. Red Guards, mobilized mainly among young people, attacked officials and intellectuals and sought to destroy the Four Olds, which often meant destroying historical artifacts and religious sites. Radical groups seized power from local governments in 1967, and their factions often fought armed clashes. Estimates of the death toll range from 1 to 2 million, and tens of millions were persecuted. Over 10 million urban youth were relocated to the countryside. In 1978 [[Deng Xiaoping]] became paramount leader and launched [[Reform and opening up|reform and opening up]]; in 1981 the Chinese Communist Party publicly acknowledged the movement's failures.

Branch of [[Anthropology|anthropology]] focused on the study of cultural variation among humans. It contrasts with [[Social anthropology|social anthropology]], which treats cultural variation as a subset of a posited anthropological constant. Anthropologists note that through culture, people adapt to their environments in non-genetic ways. The term was coined by the [[Franz Boas|Boas]] circle, whose cultural relativism and historical particularism shaped the field. Its [[Methodology|research methods]] include participant observation, often called fieldwork, along with interviews and surveys. Much of its theory concerns the tension between local, particular cultures and a universal human nature.

Adoption by a [[Minority group|minority group]] or culture of the values, behaviors, and beliefs of a majority society. Assimilation is opposed to [[Multiculturalism|multiculturalism]], which promotes the coexistence and preservation of multiple cultures. By contrast, cultural integration describes becoming economically and socially integrated while retaining elements of one's original [[Culture|culture]]. Full assimilation can occur spontaneously, while forced assimilation is imposed, as during colonialism in the 18th, 19th, and 20th centuries, through religious conversion, separation of families, and loss of local economies. Assimilationism names government policies that deliberately assimilate ethnic groups into a national culture. Whether minority groups should be expected to assimilate is disputed both by those groups and by dominant society, and [[Discrimination|discrimination]] can hinder the process.

Tangible and intangible legacy of a society inherited from past generations. Heritage is a product of selection by society, so not all legacies of the past qualify. Tangible heritage includes buildings, monuments, archival documents, books, artworks, and artifacts. Intangible heritage includes [[Folklore|folklore]], traditions, [[Language|language]], and knowledge, and natural heritage includes landscapes and [[Biodiversity|biodiversity]]. Preservation, as it is called in American English (conservation in British English), keeps heritage for future generations, and [[Museum|museums]] and cultural centers promote it. Preserved heritage is an anchor of the global [[Tourism|tourism]] industry. [[UNESCO]], the [[United Nations]], and Blue Shield International are involved in its protection, which rests on international agreements and national laws.

Turkic nomadic people from [[Central Asia]], the western branch of the Cuman–Kipchak confederation. Rus' chronicles called them Polovtsians, and Eastern sources called them Kipchaks. They inhabited a shifting area north of the [[Black Sea]] and along the [[Volga]] River, known as Cumania. Many settled west of the Black Sea, where Cuman immigrants became integrated into the elites of [[Kievan Rus']], the [[Second Bulgarian Empire]], the [[Kingdom of Hungary|Kingdom of Hungary]], and the [[Byzantine Empire]]. After the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus' in 1237, many Cumans sought asylum in Hungary. The Cuman language, the best-known of the early [[Turkic languages]], survives in the Codex Cumanicus, a linguistic manual written to help Catholic missionaries communicate with the Cuman people.

Ceremonial county in North West England (pop., 2024: 510,680). Predominantly rural, it borders [[Scotland]] to the north and the [[Irish Sea]] to the west, and its largest settlement is Carlisle. The [[Lake District]] in the southwest, a national park and [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]], includes England's highest mountain, Scafell Pike. [[Hadrian's Wall]] runs through the north of the county. Cumbria was created in 1974 from Cumberland, Westmorland, the Furness area of [[Lancashire]], and a small part of [[Yorkshire]].

Annual flowering plant of the [[Apiaceae|parsley family]], whose dried seeds are used as a [[Spice|spice]]. Native to the Irano-Turanian region, *Cuminum cyminum* has been used for thousands of years, and [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptians]] used it as a spice and in mummification. It was significant to the Minoans of [[Crete]] and was used heavily in [[Rome|ancient Roman]] cuisine. Today it is grown mostly in the [[Indian subcontinent]], North Africa, Mexico, Chile, and China. Whole or ground seeds flavor the [[Cuisine|cuisines]] of many cultures, and cumin is used in [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]], though there is no high-quality evidence that it is safe or effective as a therapeutic agent.

Metamorphic amphibole silicate, (Mg,Fe²⁺)₇Si₈O₂₂(OH)₂. Monoclinic cummingtonite is polymorphic with the more common orthorhombic anthophyllite, and it forms a solid-solution series with grunerite, its iron-rich end member. The mineral is named after Cummington, Massachusetts, where it was discovered in 1824. It is also found in [[Scotland]], Sweden, South Africa, and New Zealand. It usually occurs in metamorphosed magnesium-rich rocks, often coexisting with [[Talc|talc]] or [[Pyroxene|pyroxene]]. The grunerite end member is characteristic of metamorphosed iron formations of the [[Lake Superior]] region.

Function giving the probability that a [[Random variable|random variable]] X takes a value less than or equal to x. Every [[Probability distribution|probability distribution]] on the real numbers is uniquely identified by such a function, which is monotone increasing, right-continuous, and approaches 0 and 1 at negative and positive infinity. For a continuous distribution, the cumulative distribution function (CDF) gives the area under the [[Probability density function|probability density function]] from negative infinity to x. CDFs are conventionally written with a capital F, and they also specify multivariate distributions.
